note: A review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 finds AI in higher education concentrated in computer science and four application areas, with little critical reflection on risks or pedagogical theory, so educators remain largely absent from shaping how these tools affect teaching and learning.
title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
authors: Olaf Zawacki‐Richter, Victoria I. Marín, Melissa Bond, Franziska Gouverneur
explain_beginner: This paper looked at many studies about artificial intelligence in universities, published between 2007 and 2018. The authors started with 2656 papers and narrowed them down to 146 for a close look. They found that most of this research comes from computer science and related fields, not from education. The tools studied mostly do four things: predict student success, grade or evaluate work, adapt to each learner, or act as tutoring systems. The paper warns that risks and ethics get little attention, and teachers are rarely involved in shaping these tools.
explain_business: This review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 shows that AI in higher education is still driven mainly by computer science and STEM researchers, with little input from educators. The tools cluster around predicting student outcomes, assessment, personalisation, and tutoring. Risks, ethics, and pedagogical theory receive scant attention. For leaders, this signals that adoption decisions should not rely on technical research alone. Investment in AI should include educators in design and governance, and should fund evaluation of ethical and teaching impact, not just deployment of prediction, assessment, or tutoring systems.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of AI in higher education, screening 2656 publications from 2007 to 2018 and synthesizing 146 articles using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Descriptive analysis showed that computer science and STEM dominate the field, and empirical work relies mostly on quantitative methods. The synthesis identified four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that critical reflection on challenges and risks is largely absent, links to pedagogical theory are weak, and ethical and educational approaches need more exploration.
